sources.title: Security considerations of the LiveView model
Assigns and HEEx templates — change tracking guide
A LiveView is a Process — The Phoenix Files

structure.rationale: Ordered around the runtime lifecycle rather than around features, per the issue's own request: process and mount first, then state and diffing (the two things that make LiveView feel reactive), then the input/output mechanics (events, async, hooks, pubsub/streams, uploads), closing on security — which reframes every prior chapter's 'client input' aside into one explicit rule.
structure.audience: Working programmers new to LiveView's internals, comfortable with Elixir and OTP basics.

claims.text: mount/3 runs twice for a fresh page load: once disconnected via the plug pipeline producing a plain HTTP response, then again after the client's websocket connects, spawning a dedicated stateful process.
connected?/1 returns true only on the connected (websocket) pass, and is the idiomatic guard for side effects like PubSub subscriptions.
A connected LiveView runs as its own BEAM process, GenServer-like, riding on a Phoenix Channel, with its own mailbox and isolated heap.
If a crash is encountered or the client connection drops, the client reconnects and mount/3 and handle_params/3 run again from scratch.

snippets.code:
def mount(_params, _session, socket) do
  if connected?(socket) do
    Phoenix.PubSub.subscribe(MyApp.PubSub, "dashboard:updates")
  end

  {:ok, assign(socket, :count, MyApp.Metrics.current_count())}
end
snippets.note: connected?/1 gating a subscription while the data fetch runs on both passes

pitfalls: Subscribing unconditionally in mount/3 subscribes the doomed disconnected-render process too.
Treating LiveView process state as durable storage rather than a cache that mount/3 must be able to rebuild.

claims.text: mount(params, session, socket) is invoked with path params and the plug session; it returns {:ok, socket} or {:ok, socket, options} where options include temporary_assigns and layout.
handle_params(params, uri, socket) runs after mount and on every live patch (push_patch or a <.link patch> click), and is where query params and URL-driven state are read.
render(assigns) is invoked whenever state changes and returns a Phoenix.LiveView.Rendered struct from a HEEx template.
live/3 in the router registers a LiveView for a path with an optional live_action atom; live_session groups routes to share one persistent connection.

snippets.code:
def mount(%{"id" => post_id}, _session, socket) do
  post = Blog.get_post!(post_id)
  {:ok, socket |> assign(:post, post) |> assign(:page_title, post.title)}
end
snippets.note: path params arrive as strings in mount/3's first argument

pitfalls: Expecting query params inside mount/3 — only path params and session are passed there; query params belong to handle_params/3.

claims.text: socket.assigns is the LiveView's only mutable state; assign/3 both updates it and marks the key as changed for the current render cycle.
Returning temporary_assigns: [key: default] from mount/3 resets that assign to the default value after every render, so the process never holds more than the latest render's value.

snippets.note: temporary assigns pattern for an unbounded, append-only list

pitfalls: Mutating socket.assigns via Map.put/3 or put_in/3 instead of assign/3, which bypasses change tracking's bookkeeping.

claims.text: HEEx templates compile into static and dynamic parts; static markup is sent once, and later renders resend only the dynamic part of an expression whose dependent assign changed.
Change tracking operates down to individual fields of a struct/map read through an assign, so @user.name changing does not force re-render of a section that only reads @user.id.
A function call performing real work (e.g. a database query) directly inside a template defeats change tracking — it re-runs on every render regardless of whether any dependent assign changed.
A local <% x = ... %> binding computed inside the template obscures its assign dependency from the compiler and defeats tracking; moving the computation into a function call preserves it.
Using a generic map function like Map.put/3 instead of assign/3 prevents the tracked update from being recognized.

pitfalls: Believing 're-renders the template' means 'resends the whole template' — the wire payload is only the changed dynamic parts.

claims.text: handle_event(event, payload, socket) handles client-originated interactions bound via phx-click, phx-submit, phx-change, etc.; payload is built client-side from phx-value-* attributes and form values.
handle_info(msg, socket) receives messages from other Elixir processes, including PubSub broadcasts; handle_cast/2 receives GenServer casts.
push_patch/2 navigates within the current LiveView and process, re-triggering handle_params/3 without remounting.
push_navigate/2 remounts a new LiveView within the same live_session without a full page reload; redirect/2 performs a full page reload and shuts down the LiveView channel.
push_event/3 dispatches a client-side 'phx:' prefixed event for a JS hook's handleEvent to receive.

pitfalls: Treating an event payload as trustworthy because the UI element that sent it was constrained — a hand-crafted payload can send anything the event name allows.

claims.text: assign_async/3 wraps a function in a linked task and assigns its result to a Phoenix.LiveView.AsyncResult, starting only once the socket is connected.
start_async/3 is the lower-level primitive; its completion (success or exit) is delivered to the handle_async/3 callback as {:ok, result} or {:exit, reason}.
cancel_async/3 kills an in-flight async task and sets its failed state.
Anything achievable with assign_async/stream_async can also be done with the lower-level start_async/handle_async pair.

snippets.note: handling both success and exit branches explicitly

pitfalls: Capturing the entire socket in an async closure instead of the specific values needed, copying far more than necessary across the process boundary.

claims.text: on_mount/1 (paired with a module's on_mount/4 callback) runs before a LiveView's own mount/3, typically wired via live_session's on_mount option for auth or shared setup.

attach_hook/4 attaches a callback to a specific stage — :handle_params, :handle_event, :handle_info, :handle_async, or :after_render — returning {:cont, socket} or {:halt, socket} (or {:halt, reply, socket} for events).

A LiveComponent has its own mount/1, update/2, render/1, and handle_event/3, but runs inside the parent LiveView's process rather than its own — the component's socket does not contain the parent's assigns, though memory is shared.
Official guidance prefers function components over LiveComponents where possible, reaching for a LiveComponent only when a piece of UI needs to encapsulate both event handling and its own state.

pitfalls: Reaching for a LiveComponent purely for code organization, when a stateless function component would do — and losing fault isolation since a LiveComponent's crash takes down the parent's whole process.

claims.text: Phoenix.PubSub.broadcast/3 delivers a message to every process subscribed to a topic, arriving in each subscriber's mailbox independently — for a LiveView, as handle_info/2.

stream(socket, name, items, opts) assigns a collection for client-side DOM management via phx-update="stream"; items render as {dom_id, item} tuples and the server does not retain the full collection after the initial render.
stream_insert/4 inserts or updates a single item (with :at and :limit options); stream_delete/3 and stream_delete_by_dom_id/3 remove items.

snippets.note: inserting a PubSub-delivered item into a stream rather than assign/3

pitfalls: Trying to read a streamed collection back out of socket.assigns for later logic — it isn't held there after the initial render.

claims.text: allow_upload/3 configures accepted file types, max entries, and max file size for a named upload; live_file_input/1 renders the file input, and phx-change plus phx-submit must be bound on the form.
Client-reported upload metadata cannot be trusted; max_file_size is enforced server-side as each chunk is actually received, not from the client's declared size.
consume_uploaded_entries/3 is the point at which an uploaded file's temporary path is available to the callback; the temp file is cleaned up afterward.
A DOM element with phx-hook must carry a unique id; hook lifecycle callbacks are mounted, beforeUpdate, updated, destroyed, disconnected, and reconnected.
Inside a hook, pushEvent(event, payload, callback) sends a client event to the LiveView, and handleEvent(event, callback) receives events pushed from the server via push_event/3.

snippets.note: moving a file out of its temp path inside the one callback where it's available

pitfalls: Trusting a client-declared content type or file size without server-side verification.

claims.text: Session validation must happen independently on both the HTTP plug pipeline leg and the stateful websocket mount, since the websocket handshake is a separate connection.
params in mount/3 and handle_params/3, and payloads in handle_event/3, are untrusted client data and must be authorized and validated server-side, the same as a controller would.

Authorization should be checked at mount (page access), handle_params (navigation targets), and handle_event (the specific action) — permissions must always be verified server-side regardless of UI restrictions.
A user remains connected to an already-open LiveView after logging out elsewhere unless the app explicitly broadcasts a disconnect on that session's live_socket_id.

snippets.note: forcing every LiveView tied to a session to disconnect (and re-run mount/3's checks) on logout

pitfalls: Relying on client-side UI restrictions (disabled buttons, hidden menu items) as if they were authorization.
Assuming an already-open LiveView tab reflects a permission change made in another session without an explicit live_socket_id disconnect.
